ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain

Zixuan Huang Equal contribution    Yang Zhou Equal contribution    Guli Zhang    Sunzhu Li    Hongyan Xie    Zehao Chen    Fuzhen Zhuang    Kaixuan Wang    Xiaozhi Chen    Yikun Ban Corresponding author    Deqing Wang Corresponding author
Abstract

Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow–fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain’s movement decisions and the action expert’s continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain’s weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow–fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

††date: 2026.11.17††correspondence: huang_zx@buaa.edu.cn

1 Introduction

VLN requires an embodied agent to connect movement decisions with precise movement Cheng et al. (2024); Qi et al. (2025); Anderson et al. (2018); Ku et al. (2020); Krantz et al. (2020); Wang et al. (2025). Representative methods adapt a general-purpose VLM through navigation-domain supervision to predict geometric goals for an action expert Wei et al. (2025a); Gong et al. (2026) or generate numerical movement commands in a predefined format Cheng et al. (2024). However, we observe substantial displacement of the base VLM’s weights and degraded performance of general visual capability following this adaptation, as shown in Figure 1.

Inspired by DeepSeek-R1-Zero Guo et al. (2025), which demonstrates that reasoning capabilities can emerge through RL directly from a base language model without prior SFT, we introduce ZeroVLN, the first slow–fast navigation framework that learns navigation through environment interaction with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than adapting the brain to predict geometric goals, we introduce a semantic tool interface that connects it to a trainable flow-matching action expert Yi et al. (2026). Through natural-language tool calls, the brain conveys movement decisions to the action expert, which translates them into continuous motion.

Within this framework, we first construct reference trajectories from the brain’s own movement requests, collected through online rollouts with the brain frozen. To ground these requests in executable motion, we design a privileged trajectory planner that leverages a semantic map derived from the scene mesh Miao et al. (2026). The resulting reference trajectories are paired with their originating requests to provide semantically aligned supervision for the action expert.

We then jointly optimize the brain’s movement decisions and the action expert’s continuous execution through multi-round agentic RL Feng et al. (2025); Zheng et al. (2026). To address sparse success signals in challenging long-horizon navigation tasks, we design complementary process and outcome rewards that distinguish useful progress even when task completion fails.

Beyond conventional slow–fast frameworks, our design provides two key benefits: (1) the semantic interface leverages the brain’s native capabilities for flexible tool use and feedback-driven recovery Yu et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026); (2) Rather than specializing the model for navigation through SFT, ZeroVLN builds upon its existing language and navigation decision-making capabilities, using RL to enhance navigation performance while largely preserving its general-purpose abilities.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce ZeroVLN, the first slow–fast VLN framework that connects a VLM brain with an action expert policy through a semantic tool interface, achieving zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain.

  • •

    We develop a two-stage training paradigm that first aligns continuous execution with the brain’s semantic requests through request-grounded supervision and execution-prefix learning, then jointly optimizes the slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL.

  • •

    Across mainstream VLN-CE benchmarks, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based baselines trained on the same navigation episodes, with only 0.01497% VLM weight displacement while largely preserving general visual capabilities.

2 Architecture

Semantic Tool Calls and Contextual Queries.

As illustrated in Figure 2, we separate movement decisions from continuous motion execution through a semantic tool-calling interface. Rather than predicting geometric goals, the VLM brain makes movement decisions via run_action_head(target, where, plan), specifying a target, its relative location, and a local plan for the action expert. The brain can also inspect the scene through turn(direction, degrees) or terminate navigation through stop(reason), with prompts and tool schemas detailed in Appendix G.1.

At slow decision round tt, the brain policy πθ\pi_{\theta} generates a tool call yty_{t} from multimodal context xtx_{t}, including the navigation instruction, RGB observations, tool history, and trajectory trace. For movement calls, qtq_{t} denotes the natural-language arguments of yty_{t}. To convey the request and its navigation context to the action expert, we concatenate learnable query embeddings QQ with the embedded context and tool call. The VLM contextualizes these queries, whose final-layer hidden states QtQ_{t} provide the action expert with semantic conditioning Wei et al. (2025a):

Qt=[VLMθ⁡(Embed⁡(xt,yt)⊕Q)]Q.Q_{t}=\left[\operatorname{VLM}_{\theta}\left(\operatorname{Embed}(x_{t},y_{t})\oplus Q\right)\right]_{Q}. (1)
Visual Execution at a Faster Timescale.

While the brain specifies the intended movement, the action expert executes the call over multiple fast cycles. Throughout each call, the semantic condition QtQ_{t} and reference image ItrefI_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}} remain fixed, while RGB observations It,kI_{t,k} are refreshed at each cycle Wei et al. (2025a). A frozen visual encoder and trainable fusion module combine both images into visual features Ft,kF_{t,k}. The semantic adapter P1P_{1} projects QtQ_{t} into the visual conditioning space and adds a semantic-channel embedding, while P2P_{2} adds a visual-channel embedding to Ft,kF_{t,k}. Concatenating the two streams forms the action expert’s conditioning input:

Ct,k=P1​(Qt)⊕P2​(Ft,k).C_{t,k}=P_{1}(Q_{t})\oplus P_{2}(F_{t,k}). (2)

Conditioned on Ct,kC_{t,k}, the continuous-action expert πϕ\pi_{\phi} integrates the flow velocities predicted by fϕf_{\phi} to generate an HH-step action sequence. After inverse normalization, each action specifies relative planar displacements and a heading change in the local frame defined by the agent’s pose at the start of each cycle. At each cycle, we execute only the first h≤Hh\leq H steps, then refresh the observation and predict the next sequence, adapting motion while preserving the brain’s intent. After each movement call, visual and trajectory feedback, including blocked motion or collisions, allows the brain to continue, inspect the scene, revise its request, or stop. Figure 3 details this execution path: NqN_{q} semantic queries and NvN_{v} visual tokens condition an LdL_{d}-layer decoder, with an LmL_{m}-layer flow-time MLP and NfN_{f} flow integration steps. Appendix B.1 provides further details on the action expert’s architecture and execution.

3 Learning to Execute Semantic Requests

Request-Grounded Anchoring.

Our semantic interface also changes how action expert supervision must be constructed. Geometric-interface VLN frameworks can derive training conditions directly from scene meshes or ground-truth trajectories Wei et al. (2025a); Gong et al. (2026); An et al. (2024), whereas our action expert follows natural-language requests issued online by the brain itself. Directly constructing semantic requests may not match the brain’s actual request distribution, leaving the action expert exposed to out-of-distribution instructions at inference. Generating requests online along fixed trajectories also leaves the action labels independent of the requested movement. We report results for these alternatives, including CAST-inspired augmentation Glossop et al. (2025) and request transfer in Appendix D.2.

Built upon these insights, we propose a request-grounded data construction strategy that generates trajectories from the brain’s actual requests. To realize this, we design a privileged semantic planner that uses a mesh-derived semantic map Miao et al. (2026) and training-only geometry to ground each request qtq_{t} at the agent’s current state sts_{t} into a reachable local goal gt⋆g_{t}^{\star}, from which a reference trajectory ρt\rho_{t} is planned. The resulting execution-verified trajectories are paired with their originating requests to provide semantically aligned supervision for action expert adaptation. Further details of the semantic planner are provided in Appendix B.2.

Execution-Prefix Supervision.

These request-grounded trajectories provide aligned training targets, but supervision must also match the action expert’s execution criteria. For each verified trajectory ρt\rho_{t}, we construct HH-step reference action chunks Ut,k⋆∈ℝH×daU_{t,k}^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}} across KK fast execution cycles, with dad_{a} action components per step, and pair them with the corresponding conditions Ct,kC_{t,k}. Additional details on action construction are provided in Appendix B.3.

Existing action-chunking methods supervise the full prediction horizon despite executing only a short prefix before replanning Wei et al. (2025a); Chi et al. (2025); Black et al. (2024). Once new observations arrive, the remaining predictions are discarded, creating a mismatch between training and execution. We therefore retain full-horizon prediction while restricting flow-matching supervision to the executed hh-step prefix. At flow time uu sampled from a logit-normal distribution, we interpolate the full reference chunk with Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), but compute the loss only over its first hh actions:

Ut,k(u)=(1−u)​Ut,k⋆+u​ϵ,ℒFM=𝔼⁡[1K​∑k=1K1h​da​∑j=1h‖[fϕ​(Ut,k(u),u,Ct,k)−(ϵ−Ut,k⋆)]j‖22].U_{t,k}^{(u)}=(1-u)U_{t,k}^{\star}+u\epsilon,\hskip 18.49988pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{hd_{a}}\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left\|\left[f_{\phi}(U_{t,k}^{(u)},u,C_{t,k})-(\epsilon-U_{t,k}^{\star})\right]_{j}\right\|_{2}^{2}\Bigg]. (3)

During this stage, the VLM brain and visual encoder remain frozen, while the learnable queries QQ and action expert parameters ϕ\phi are optimized.

4 Joint Slow–Fast Optimization via Agentic RL

4.1 Trajectory-Level Credit Assignment

Supervised adaptation enables the action expert policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} to execute individual movement requests, while successful navigation also depends on the VLM brain’s ability to make movement decisions through semantic tool calls.

To jointly improve movement decisions and continuous execution, we optimize the VLM brain policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and action expert policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} using navigation feedback through closed-loop agentic RL Feng et al. (2025); Zheng et al. (2026). Accurately estimating round-level advantages is challenging because task success depends on decisions and execution across multi-round interaction with the environment. We instead adopt trajectory-level credit assignment to evaluate their combined contribution to navigation success.

For each navigation task, we sample GG independent long-horizon rollouts, with rollout ii comprising TiT_{i} rounds of tool calls, corresponding action executions, and per-round environment feedback, which is used to compute the reward for each round. Using RLOO advantage estimation Ahmadian et al. (2024); Shao et al. (2024), we compute the advantage AiA_{i} by comparing its cumulative return RiR_{i} with the mean return of the remaining G−1G-1 rollouts:

Ri=∑t=0Ti−1ri,t,Ai=Ri−1G−1​∑j≠iRj.R_{i}=\sum_{t=0}^{T_{i}-1}r_{i,t},\hskip 18.49988ptA_{i}=R_{i}-\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\neq i}R_{j}. (4)

We use the same advantage AiA_{i} to update both policies across all rounds of rollout ii, jointly improving semantic decisions and continuous execution for navigation success.

4.2 Process and Outcome Rewards

For challenging long-horizon navigation tasks, terminal success alone provides sparse supervision across the many decisions and actions made over multiple interaction rounds. We incorporate additional rewards derived from environment feedback at each interaction round. By distinguishing intermediate progress across rollouts, these rewards preserve relative learning signals even when no rollout reaches the goal, mitigating gradient degeneration when all rollouts fail:

rt=wsucc​rtsucc+warr​rtarr+wprog​rtprog+winfo​rtinfo.r_{t}=w_{\mathrm{succ}}r_{t}^{\mathrm{succ}}+w_{\mathrm{arr}}r_{t}^{\mathrm{arr}}+w_{\mathrm{prog}}r_{t}^{\mathrm{prog}}+w_{\mathrm{info}}r_{t}^{\mathrm{info}}. (5)
Terminal Success.

We reward task success in the interaction round where it is confirmed by the environment’s native success criterion:

rtsucc=St,r_{t}^{\mathrm{succ}}=S_{t}, (6)

where St∈{0,1}S_{t}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether task success is confirmed at round tt of rollout ii.

First Arrival.

We reward the agent once when it first enters the goal region, which provides an outcome signal that is easier to obtain than terminal success. Let ηt−\eta^{-}_{t} and ηt+\eta^{+}_{t} indicate whether the goal has ever been reached before and after a call, respectively:

rtarr=(1−ηt−)​ηt+.r_{t}^{\mathrm{arr}}=(1-\eta^{-}_{t})\eta^{+}_{t}. (7)
Distance Progress.

On challenging navigation tasks, both terminal success and first arrival can be difficult to achieve. We use process rewards to distinguish productive behavior even when neither outcome reward is obtained. We measure progress through a bounded proximity potential based on traversable distance d⁡(s)d(s) to the goal region. For each rollout ii, we set the distance scale D=max⁡(d⁡(s0),dmin)D=\max(d(s_{0}),d_{\min}) from its initial state s0s_{0}, using dmin>0d_{\min}>0 as a lower bound. We then compute rtprogr_{t}^{\mathrm{prog}} as the increase in goal proximity from the pre-call state st−s^{-}_{t} to the post-call state st+s^{+}_{t}:

rtprog=DD+d⁡(st+)−DD+d⁡(st−).r_{t}^{\mathrm{prog}}=\frac{D}{D+d(s^{+}_{t})}-\frac{D}{D+d(s^{-}_{t})}. (8)
Information Discovery.

Distance progress alone overlooks active observation that reveals useful navigation cues without immediate movement toward the goal. We therefore reward newly discovered, depth-verified task-relevant entities. After each call, we count newly discovered entities ntn_{t} by excluding the previously observed set 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t}, including the initial view, from the currently visible set 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}. We add these discoveries to the pre-call cumulative count ctc_{t} and reward its increase up to a total of NinfoN_{\mathrm{info}} discoveries:

nt=|𝒱t∖𝒮t|,rtinfo=min⁡(Ninfo,ct+nt)−min⁡(Ninfo,ct).n_{t}=|\mathcal{V}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{t}|,\hskip 18.49988ptr_{t}^{\mathrm{info}}=\min(N_{\mathrm{info}},c_{t}+n_{t})-\min(N_{\mathrm{info}},c_{t}). (9)

4.3 Joint Policy Optimization

Tool Policy Optimization.

We optimize the VLM brain policy πθ\pi_{\theta} using a REINFORCE objective Ahmadian et al. (2024); Li et al. (2023) with rollouts sampled from the current policy to improve movement decisions through semantic tool calls. We weight the mean log-probability of sampled response tokens by the trajectory-level advantage AiA_{i}:

ℓ¯i,ttext=1|𝒯i,t|∑n∈𝒯i,tlogπθ(yi,t,n∣xi,t,yi,t,<n),ℒtext=−λtextB∑i1Ti∑tsg(Ai)ℓ¯i,ttext.\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{text}}_{i,t}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i,t}|}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{T}_{i,t}}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t,n}\mid x_{i,t},y_{i,t,<n}),\hskip 18.49988pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{text}}=-\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{text}}}{B}\sum_{i}\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t}\operatorname{sg}(A_{i})\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{text}}_{i,t}. (10)

For each round, we average token log-probabilities over the sampled response positions 𝒯i,t\mathcal{T}_{i,t}. We weight this mean by sg⁡(Ai)\operatorname{sg}(A_{i}), holding the trajectory advantage constant during backpropagation, then average over rounds within each rollout and the BB rollouts in the batch.

Action Policy Optimization.

We optimize the action expert policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} through policy gradients over sampled Flow-SDE paths, following Flow-GRPO and DPPO Liu et al. (2026); Ren et al. (2025). We clip the trajectory advantage to obtain Aiexec=clip⁡(Ai,−amax,amax)A_{i}^{\mathrm{exec}}=\operatorname{clip}(A_{i},-a_{\max},a_{\max}) using threshold amaxa_{\max} and use it to weight the path log-likelihood ℓi,t,kexec\ell^{\mathrm{exec}}_{i,t,k} at execution cycle kk:

∇Q,ϕℒaction=−𝔼i,t,k​[sg⁡(Aiexec)​∇Q,ϕℓi,t,kexec].\nabla_{Q,\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}=-\mathbb{E}_{i,t,k}\!\left[\operatorname{sg}(A_{i}^{\mathrm{exec}})\nabla_{Q,\phi}\ell^{\mathrm{exec}}_{i,t,k}\right]. (11)

We hold AiexecA_{i}^{\mathrm{exec}} constant during backpropagation and average the weighted path gradients over cycles within each movement call, calls within each rollout, and then rollouts.

Joint Update with Separate Gradient Paths.

We couple the slow and fast policies through the shared trajectory-level advantage, so that both semantic tool calls and action execution are optimized toward the overall navigation objective. Meanwhile, we maintain separate gradient paths:

gθ=∇θℒtext,gQ,ϕ=∇Q,ϕℒaction.g_{\theta}=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{text}},\hskip 18.49988ptg_{Q,\phi}=\nabla_{Q,\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}. (12)

In this way, joint RL coordinates both policies through shared navigation feedback while preventing action-policy gradients from directly altering the brain’s tool-call distribution. We provide the complete algorithm in Algorithm 4.3 and detailed optimization objectives in Appendices B.4–B.6.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Evaluation.

We evaluate ZeroVLN on three mainstream VLN-CE benchmarks: SAGE-Bench Miao et al. (2026), R2R-CE Anderson et al. (2018); Krantz et al. (2020), and RxR-CE Ku et al. (2020). We restrict navigation training to a shared pool of only 34,445 episodes, used for action expert adaptation with the VLM brain frozen and sampled at every RL training step. For action expert adaptation, we generate request-grounded reference trajectories spanning multiple distance scales, as shown in Figure 5.

Following the official criteria, SAGE-Bench counts reaching the goal region as success, whereas R2R-CE and RxR-CE additionally require stopping there. We report success rate (SR), success weighted by path length (SPL) to measure path efficiency, and, for R2R-CE and RxR-CE, navigation error (NE) as the final distance to the goal and oracle success rate (OSR) as success based on any goal-region visit. Full evaluations use the official evaluation sets with a 200-round limit per episode. During RL training, we additionally evaluate every 4 training steps on 100 fixed episodes per benchmark, each with a 100-round limit.

Model and Training Details.

We pair a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B VLM brain Qwen Team (2026b) with a 12-layer flow-matching action expert using the Qwen3.5-4B vision encoder Qwen Team (2026a). For expert adaptation, we train the contextual queries and action expert for approximately 2 epochs with the brain and visual encoder frozen, using a batch size of 64 request–trajectory pairs and a constant learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}. We set the action prediction horizon H=16H=16 and the execution prefix h=4h=4. For closed-loop RL, we jointly train the brain, contextual queries, and action expert for 200 training steps, keeping the visual encoder frozen. We use a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6} and a global batch of 512 long-horizon rollouts per training step (8 rollouts for each of 64 episodes). Further details are provided in Appendices B.2 and D.1.

Baselines.

We compare ZeroVLN with training-free tool use and representative SFT-based VLN methods. Direct Tool Use equips the base VLM brain with primitive movement, turning, and stopping tools. For controlled comparisons, we train NaVILA and DualVLN on the same backbone and training episodes as ZeroVLN. NaVILA fine-tunes the VLM to predict numerical motion commands, whereas DualVLN fine-tunes it to predict pixel goals for a continuous-action expert. We provide baseline implementation and training details in Appendices D.3 and D.4.

5.2 Main Results

5.2.1 Learning to Navigate While Preserving General Capabilities

ZeroVLN achieves competitive navigation performance with substantially fewer training episodes. As shown in Table 1, ZeroVLN learns navigation from 34,445 training episodes without dataset-provided expert trajectories or navigation-domain supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the VLM brain. On SAGE-3D, it achieves 51.3% SR, surpassing NaVILA-SAGE’s 46.0% with roughly 1/14 as many training episodes. On R2R and RxR, ZeroVLN surpasses Uni-NaVid by 13.4% and 9.1% in OSR, respectively, with corresponding SR gains of 5.7% and 2.7%. Together, these results demonstrate that ZeroVLN offers a data-efficient alternative to navigation-specific brain adaptation while achieving competitive VLN-CE performance.

ZeroVLN outperforms SFT-based VLN frameworks with the same backbone and training data. DualVLN has to learn both geometric goal prediction and action execution Wei et al. (2025a), while NaVILA Cheng et al. (2024) benefits from a simpler training setup, as its predicted motion commands are executed directly by the simulator without requiring a learned action controller. This helps explain its consistently stronger performance than DualVLN across all benchmarks and metrics. Despite also learning continuous action control like DualVLN, ZeroVLN avoids requiring the VLM brain to learn a navigation-specific output interface. Instead, request-grounded supervision teaches the action expert to execute the brain’s natural-language requests, while joint RL further aligns semantic decisions with continuous execution. Under the same backbone and training episodes, ZeroVLN outperforms DualVLN by over 30% in SR across all three benchmarks. Notably, it also surpasses NaVILA, whose motion commands are executed directly by the simulator without a learned action controller, by 27.8%, 6.2%, and 2.7% on SAGE-3D, R2R, and RxR, respectively.

The flexibility of semantic tool use comes with a trade-off in path efficiency. On R2R and RxR, ZeroVLN achieves higher OSR than NaVILA (66.7% and 64.6% vs. 51.8% and 55.6%), but lower SPL (29.2% and 28.1% vs. 41.8% and 43.0%). Rather than imitating dataset-provided expert trajectories, ZeroVLN learns through interaction, allowing the agent to recover from blocked movement by revising its requests and exploring alternative paths. This flexibility improves goal reachability, although the additional exploration can lead to longer navigation paths and lower SPL.

ZeroVLN learns navigation while largely preserving the VLM brain’s general capabilities. As illustrated in Figure 6, Navigation SFT reshapes the brain’s output distribution to fit navigation-specific targets, whereas our joint RL reinforces or suppresses the brain’s own sampled tool-call token paths according to trajectory-level advantages.

This distinction in training signals is reflected in the extent of VLM parameter changes. As shown in Figure 7, ZeroVLN induces only 0.01497% relative VLM weight displacement Ilharco et al. (2022); Xuhong et al. (2018), compared with 3.21% for DualVLN and 7.67% for NaVILA. This substantially smaller parameter shift is accompanied by stronger retention of general visual capabilities. In a spatial reasoning example, both the base and ZeroVLN-tuned brains correctly identify the tray as the nearest object, whereas DualVLN and NaVILA generate navigation commands. Such cases are not isolated. Across twelve general visual benchmarks, ZeroVLN retains 59.16% mean accuracy, close to the base brain’s 59.47%, while both SFT baselines score zero. These qualitative and quantitative results jointly demonstrate that ZeroVLN can acquire navigation capabilities with minimal changes to the VLM brain while largely preserving its general visual capabilities. Further theoretical analysis and complete evaluation results are presented in Appendix C and  E.1, respectively.

To test whether the zero scores reflect only failures to follow answer instructions, we sample 100 multiple-choice questions from each of seven benchmarks. After a fixed Answer: prefix, we read the probabilities of answer option tokens directly from the model’s next-token vocabulary distribution. We select the most probable option without requiring the model to generate a formatted answer. As shown in Figure 8, NaVILA and DualVLN perform close to the random baseline on every benchmark. By contrast, ZeroVLN achieves 62.00% accuracy, close to the base brain’s 62.86%. These results reveal severe degradation beyond instruction following: the general visual capabilities encoded in the models’ parameters also deteriorate substantially on these tasks.

5.2.2 Why Does ZeroVLN Work?

The Base Brain Already Makes Useful Navigation Decisions. As shown in Table 1, Direct Tool Use achieves 39.5% SR on SAGE-3D without navigation training, demonstrating that a general-purpose VLM can already leverage instructions and visual observations to make useful navigation decisions, which provides the foundation for our request-grounded supervision.

Execution-Prefix Action Expert Adaptation Provides a Strong Initialization for RL. As shown in Figure 9, semantically aligned action adaptation raises SR from 27.0% to 37.5% on SAGE-3D and from 11.6% to 17.4% on average across R2R and RxR. The supervision strategy also matters: on identical reference trajectories, execution-prefix supervision consistently outperforms full-sequence supervision, validating its better alignment with actual execution. The adapted policy achieves a mean Pass@4 of 43.5% on R2R/RxR, improving the likelihood of sampling successful rollouts. This provides a stronger exploration policy for group-relative RL, mitigating degenerate advantage estimates under sparse terminal rewards.

Joint RL Translates Local Execution into End-to-End Navigation Success. While supervised adaptation teaches the action expert to follow individual movement requests, successful navigation requires coordinating successive semantic decisions and continuous executions. As shown in Table 1, joint RL raises SR from 17.0% to 52.7% on R2R, from 18.7% to 51.4% on RxR, and from 36.9% to 51.3% on SAGE-3D. The staircase example in Figure 10 illustrates this multi-round coordination. After encountering blocked motion, the brain changes its view and revises its movement request, which the action expert executes to reach the second landing before the brain successfully stops. This demonstrates how coordinated semantic decisions and continuous execution support recovery from local failures and successful completion of long-horizon navigation tasks.

5.3 Ablation Studies

Trajectory-level advantages favor task completion and path efficiency, whereas round-level advantages emphasize goal reaching. We compare the two credit assignment strategies under identical reward settings. As shown in Figure 11, round-level advantages achieve higher OSR but exhibit declining SR and increasing NE during training, whereas trajectory-level advantages yield higher SR and SPL with lower NE, indicating more reliable task completion and better path efficiency despite fewer goal visits. The key difference lies in how credit is assigned. Round-level advantages can reinforce a goal-reaching decision even if subsequent actions lead to failure, whereas trajectory-level advantages assign all rounds the same advantage derived from the complete navigation return. By accounting for both goal arrival and terminal success, trajectory-level credit favors decisions that contribute to successful task completion rather than isolated goal visits. Implementation details of the round-level variant are provided in Appendix B.7.

Joint optimization enables coordinated adaptation of movement decisions and action execution. As shown in Figure 12 (top), updating only the action expert yields limited improvements, suggesting that better execution alone cannot overcome the limitations of fixed semantic decisions. In contrast, updating only the brain initially improves navigation, but SR and OSR subsequently decline below initialization. This behavior is consistent with a growing mismatch between the brain’s evolving movement requests and the fixed action expert. Joint RL, however, achieves sustained improvements across navigation metrics by allowing both policies to adapt together. These results highlight the importance of coordinated slow–fast optimization: improving either policy in isolation is insufficient when successful navigation depends on their continued alignment. Figure 13 (top) confirms this pattern under round-level credit: Joint RL improves SR and SPL beyond updating either policy alone.

Each component of our reward design plays a significant role in sustaining stable navigation learning. We ablate each reward component under fixed trajectory-level credit assignment, as shown in Figure 12 (bottom). (1) Ablation of Outcome Rewards. Removing the first-arrival reward severely degrades navigation performance across metrics, particularly OSR, demonstrating that the sparsity of terminal success rewards makes it difficult to learn effective goal-reaching behavior without denser intermediate feedback. The first-arrival reward bridges this gap by providing a more immediate signal upon reaching the goal. Conversely, without terminal success, OSR remains high while other metrics deteriorate, suggesting that rewarding arrival alone encourages goal visits rather than successful termination. These results demonstrate that the two outcome rewards must work together to balance goal reaching and task completion. (2) Ablation of Process Rewards. The process rewards further support learning when outcome rewards are scarce. Distance progress guides movement toward the goal, while information discovery encourages useful observation even without immediate spatial progress. Removing either weakens or destabilizes training, demonstrating their complementary roles in sustaining navigation improvement. We observe consistent trends under round-level credit assignment in Figure 13, further supporting the complementary roles of goal-reaching and completion rewards.

5.4 Consistency between Predicted Trajectories and Planner Goals

We assess the consistency between predicted trajectories and planner-grounded local goals before and after joint RL. Under identical observations and noise seeds, we measure the endpoint distances and angular deviations of predicted action sequences relative to the local goals. As shown in Figure 14, both stages exhibit low endpoint distances and angular deviations, demonstrating that supervised adaptation establishes goal-following behavior that is largely preserved after joint RL.

6 Conclusion

We introduce ZeroVLN, the first slow–fast VLN framework that enables a general-purpose VLM brain to guide action expert execution through semantic tool use, without navigation-domain SFT. We combine request-grounded and execution-prefix supervision with joint agentic RL, achieving strong navigation performance with limited data while largely preserving the VLM’s general capabilities. Beyond navigation, this paradigm opens a path toward general-purpose embodied agents that acquire diverse physical skills through specialized action experts while retaining a shared VLM brain.
