Appendix A Related Work

Slow–Fast Systems for Navigation.

Slow–fast architectures separate semantic planning from motion execution, allowing each policy to operate at its own timescale. Mobility VLA Chiang et al. (2024) uses a long-context VLM to select a goal frame from a demonstration tour and a topological navigation policy to reach it. NavGPT-2 Zhou et al. (2024a) connects a frozen language model’s vision-language representations to a navigation policy network. DualVLN Wei et al. (2025a) trains its planner to predict pixel goals before learning contextual queries and a flow-matching action expert. ABot-N1 Gong et al. (2026) similarly uses supervised reasoning and affordance pixels to guide a fast waypoint predictor. Beyond navigation, SmolVLA Shukor et al. (2025) decouples action prediction and execution through asynchronous inference, while Fast-in-Slow Chen et al. (2025a) partially shares parameters between slow reasoning and fast manipulation and coordinates them through dual-aware co-training. ZeroVLN retains this separation of planning and execution but connects the two policies through semantic requests, avoiding navigation-domain SFT for geometric goal prediction.

Navigation Planning with Existing Executors.

Navigation agents can use language-model reasoning to select actions executed by an external system. NavGPT Zhou et al. (2024b) reasons over textual observations, navigation history, and candidate directions, while MapGPT Chen et al. (2024) adds a linguistic map and adaptive multi-step planning. SayNav Rajvanshi et al. (2024) grounds language-model plans in an incrementally constructed 3D scene graph and delegates their execution to an existing low-level navigation policy. AgenticNav Li et al. (2026) exposes movement, depth, and memory as callable tools, with the harness converting selected image pixels into executable motion. NaVILA Cheng et al. (2024) instead predicts numerical movement commands in language. In the VLN-CE simulation setting considered here, these commands are executed by the system. Its legged-robot setting additionally uses a learned visual locomotion policy. ETP-R1 Ye et al. (2025) applies closed-loop GRPO to topological planning while retaining the underlying controller. Beyond selecting calls to an existing executor, ZeroVLN learns the executor itself by treating the continuous-action head as a trainable tool.

Privileged Supervision for Navigation Action Policies.

Privileged geometry can supervise motion without requiring a human demonstration for every observation. For high-speed flight, Loquercio et al. Loquercio et al. (2021) train a sensorimotor policy in simulation by imitating a privileged expert, mapping onboard observations directly to collision-free trajectories. iPlanner Yang et al. (2023) backpropagates trajectory costs through a differentiable geometric costmap, while ViPlanner Roth et al. (2024) incorporates semantic costs to distinguish traversable surfaces and obstacles. NavDP Cai et al. (2025) uses privileged simulation information to learn both trajectory generation and critic-based trajectory evaluation from local RGB-D observations. CAST Glossop et al. (2025) addresses instruction following by constructing counterfactual instruction–action labels from existing robot data. In contrast, ZeroVLN starts from the brain’s actual movement requests and uses a privileged trajectory planner to generate matching reference trajectories.

Agentic RL and Credit Assignment.

DeepSeek-R1 Guo et al. (2025), DAPO Yu et al. (2026), and GSPO Zheng et al. (2025) improve language-model reasoning through RL. SAGE Huang et al. (2026a) targets reasoning efficiency, while R2M Huang et al. (2026b) aligns reward feedback with the evolving policy. Extending RL to multi-round agents requires connecting delayed outcomes to the decisions that produced them. ReTool Feng et al. (2026) interleaves language reasoning with code execution and uses outcome rewards to learn when and how to invoke tools. GiGPO Feng et al. (2025) combines episode-level advantages with step-level comparisons at repeated environment states. PGPO Zheng et al. (2026) estimates state potentials from grouped rollout returns to distinguish intermediate actions. Agent Lightning Luo et al. (2025) decomposes agent trajectories into training transitions, while Agent-R1 Cheng et al. (2025) separates generated outputs from environment feedback during policy optimization. VAGEN Wang et al. (2026) introduces explicit world-model reasoning and bi-level credit assignment for visually grounded agents. In autonomous driving, DEFT-RLVR Huang et al. (2026c) combines verifiable trajectory selection with rubric-based reasoning rewards, assigning shared credit across its two-stage interaction. ZeroVLN adapts trajectory-level credit to navigation through complementary process and outcome rewards that account for exploration, goal reaching, and task completion.

Reinforcement Learning for Generative Action Policies.

Generative action policies require optimization through their action-generation process. Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization Ren et al. (2025) applies policy gradients to diffusion denoising steps for continuous control. Flow-GRPO Liu et al. (2026) converts deterministic flow sampling into stochastic paths to enable online group-relative optimization, providing a mechanism applicable to flow-based action generation. Flow Policy Gradients Yi et al. (2026) instead optimizes expressive flow policies without explicit likelihood computation for robot control. ConRFT Chen et al. (2025b) combines behavior cloning and Q-learning for offline VLA adaptation, followed by online consistency-policy optimization with human interventions. RIPT-VLA Tan et al. (2025) uses interactive rollouts and leave-one-out advantages to adapt VLA policies from sparse success rewards. Building on action-policy RL, ZeroVLN is, to our knowledge, the first to jointly optimize a VLM brain and a continuous-action expert through agentic RL in VLN-CE.

History Modeling and Spatial Planning.

Navigation policies use history to maintain spatial context beyond the current observation. HAMT Chen et al. (2021) jointly encodes the instruction, past panoramic observations, and current view. DUET Chen et al. (2022) combines local visual grounding with a global topological map for long-range planning. BEVBert An et al. (2022) learns multimodal map representations that combine local metric structure with global topology, supporting spatial reasoning and long-range planning. GridMM Wang et al. (2023) organizes historical observations in an egocentric grid memory and aggregates instruction-relevant visual features. ETPNav An et al. (2024) constructs an online topological map from predicted waypoints and couples cross-modal planning with an obstacle-avoiding controller. ZeroVLN likewise retains historical context, but supplies interaction records and the executed trajectory trace directly to the brain for semantic tool decisions.

Appendix B Additional Details of Model Architecture and Training Paradigm

B.1 Action Expert Architecture

Figure 3 illustrates our action expert. We provide all numerical settings and parameter counts in Appendix D.1, including Tables 2 and 3. The architecture follows the dual-stream conditioning design of DualVLN Wei et al. (2025a). Our implementation uses a query-based visual pooler and a condition-fusion Transformer to combine the movement request with reference and current views.

Fusing Reference and Current Views.

The frozen encoder EψE_{\psi} extracts visual tokens from the reference image ItrefI_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}}, captured at the start of the movement call, and the refreshed image It,kI_{t,k}. A shared linear projection maps both token sequences to the action expert’s conditioning dimension. We add separate learned temporal embeddings to distinguish the reference and current views, concatenate the sequences, and apply a Transformer encoder. Learnable visual queries then cross-attend to the fused tokens, with a query residual connection and layer normalization, producing the fixed-length visual representation Ft,kF_{t,k}. The reference image and semantic condition QtQ_{t} remain fixed within the call, while current-view tokens are refreshed at each execution cycle.

Combining Semantic and Visual Conditions.

The NqN_{q} learnable queries have VLM hidden dimension dvd_{v}. Their final-layer states form the semantic condition QtQ_{t} in Eq. (1). The operator ⊕\oplus concatenates tokens, and [⋅]Q[\cdot]_{Q} selects the hidden states at the query positions. In Eq. (2), P1P_{1} applies layer normalization, a linear projection, output normalization, and a learned semantic-channel embedding to QtQ_{t}. Since Ft,kF_{t,k} is already in the conditioning space, P2P_{2} adds a learned visual-channel embedding without a further linear projection. Their concatenation Ct,kC_{t,k} forms the input to a condition-fusion Transformer within fϕf_{\phi}, which mixes the semantic and visual tokens before velocity prediction. The input queries QQ are optimized separately from the action expert parameters ϕ\phi.

Generating Actions through Flow Matching.

We linearly embed the noisy actions and add a learned position embedding for each of the HH action steps. A separate projection maps the fused conditions to the decoder width. A sinusoidal flow-time encoding followed by an MLP supplies a flow-time token, which is appended to the conditioning tokens to form the cross-attention memory. Each decoder block applies action self-attention, cross-attention to this memory, and a feedforward network, with pre-layer normalization and residual connections. A final layer normalization and linear projection predict a dad_{a}-dimensional flow velocity at each action step. Starting from Gaussian noise, flow integration produces the normalized action sequence. Inverse normalization recovers displacement and heading increments for execution.

Action Execution and Feedback.

Within each execution cycle, the predicted displacement and heading increments share the fixed local frame at the cycle’s starting pose. We accumulate these increments into target poses and convert each target into a motion command using the agent’s actual pose during execution. The coordinate frame is reset at the next cycle. Training targets follow the same convention, as detailed in Appendix B.3. Each movement call returns the latest RGB observation obtained at the end of execution, together with executed motion and execution status. Reported cumulative motion is relative to the call’s starting pose. The trajectory trace records the executed path and current heading and highlights blocked motion and collisions, providing spatial history for subsequent tool decisions.

B.2 Request Grounding and Reference Trajectory Planning

Grounding Requests in Reachable Goals.

As illustrated in Figure 2 (I-a), our privileged semantic planner grounds the brain’s movement request qtq_{t} in a reachable local goal gt⋆g_{t}^{\star} using the agent state sts_{t}, a mesh-derived semantic map, and training-only geometry. Dependency parsing extracts the target noun phrase, egocentric direction, and spatial relations from target, where, and the current movement stage of plan. Lexical matching and a frozen text encoder retrieve matching object categories and mesh instances. We restrict the search to nearby instances supported by current or historical observations, then rank the candidates lexicographically by current depth-supported visibility, direction agreement, spatial-relation support, semantic match, and increasing distance to the object’s bounding-box surface. These signals prioritize candidates rather than acting as independent rejection rules. We test candidates in this order and retain the first whose approach endpoint and reference route pass the geometric checks below.

For the current request qtq_{t}, we omit round indices on intermediate planner quantities. For each object instance ee, we sample approach positions around its bounding-box boundary at increasing offsets from a preferred standoff distance d0d_{0}. We form the candidate set 𝒜⁡(e)\mathcal{A}(e) by removing occupied positions and positions unreachable from sts_{t}. For each remaining position gg, we compute the planned route length L⁡(g)L(g), test ground-plane line of sight to the object with the binary indicator ve​(g)v_{e}(g), and measure the distance de​(g)d_{e}(g) to its bounding box. The selected approach position balances travel, geometric visibility, and proximity:

g⁡(e)=arg​ming∈𝒜⁡(e)⁡[L⁡(g)+λv​(1−ve​(g))+λd​max⁡(0,de​(g)−d0)].g(e)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{g\in\mathcal{A}(e)}\left[L(g)+\lambda_{v}\bigl(1-v_{e}(g)\bigr)+\lambda_{d}\max\bigl(0,d_{e}(g)-d_{0}\bigr)\right]. (13)

The weights λv\lambda_{v} and λd\lambda_{d} control the visibility and distance penalties, respectively. The ground-plane visibility term is a soft geometric preference, distinct from the depth-supported camera visibility used in candidate ranking. An object is rejected if its selected endpoint exceeds the maximum allowed distance from its bounding box or its route violates the spatial constraints. Denoting the remaining geometrically verified instances by ℰ\mathcal{E}, the ranking and endpoint selection together anchor the request to the local goal:

e⋆=lex​arg​maxe∈ℰ⁡(Vis⁡(e),Dir⁡(e),Rel⁡(e),Match⁡(e),−Dist⁡(e)),gt⋆=g⁡(e⋆).e^{\star}=\operatorname*{lex\,arg\,max}_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\bigl(\operatorname{Vis}(e),\operatorname{Dir}(e),\operatorname{Rel}(e),\operatorname{Match}(e),-\operatorname{Dist}(e)\bigr),\hskip 18.49988ptg_{t}^{\star}=g(e^{\star}). (14)

The five ranking terms follow the visibility, direction, relation, semantic-match, and surface-distance criteria described above. Figure 4 illustrates how “decorative painting” is associated with its mesh instance and a nearby approach endpoint.

Doorway and room requests instead use mapped openings and their adjacent room identities to construct ordered waypoints before, within, and beyond the selected opening. Routes that cross unrelated rooms are rejected. If no object target is reachable but the request specifies an egocentric direction, the planner progressively shortens the displacement along that direction until it finds a collision-free endpoint without an unintended room crossing or a substantial directional detour. Requests without a feasible object, passage, or directional target are rejected.

Reference Trajectory Planning and Verification.

For each candidate goal gg, we search an occupancy grid whose traversable cells provide sufficient clearance for the agent’s footprint. Diagonal transitions are allowed only when both neighboring cardinal cells are traversable, preventing corner cutting. To discourage routes that hug obstacles, we penalize edges whose minimum endpoint clearance Clr⁡(a,b)\operatorname{Clr}(a,b) falls below the preferred clearance c0c_{0}. A* search Hart et al. (1968) selects a grid path P⋆​(g)P^{\star}(g) from the feasible paths 𝒫⁡(g)\mathcal{P}(g) connecting the position in sts_{t} to gg by minimizing

P⋆(g)=arg​minP∈𝒫⁡(g)∑(a,b)∈P∥b−a∥2[1+λc(max⁡(0,c0−Clr⁡(a,b))c0)2].P^{\star}(g)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{P\in\mathcal{P}(g)}\sum_{(a,b)\in P}\|b-a\|_{2}\left[1+\lambda_{c}\left(\frac{\max(0,c_{0}-\operatorname{Clr}(a,b))}{c_{0}}\right)^{2}\right]. (15)

The weight λc\lambda_{c} controls the clearance penalty. If the resulting path exceeds the allowed relative length increase over the ordinary shortest grid path, we use the latter to limit detours. The resulting route length supplies L⁡(g)L(g) in Eq. (13), coupling target selection to physical reachability and execution cost.

We simplify the selected route only when shortcuts remain collision-free and preserve its clearance cost, then apply spline smoothing and uniform arc-length resampling. Smoothing keeps both endpoints fixed and is progressively weakened if the curve exceeds the allowed increase in path length or reduction in minimum clearance, or violates the agent’s footprint clearance. Every point and connecting segment must pass collision checks, otherwise the original safe polyline is retained. Stair requests use the native three-dimensional navigation mesh, with height changes constrained to the matched stair flight and requested ascending or descending direction. The verified geometry is converted into the reference trajectory ρt:[0,Lt]→𝒮\rho_{t}:[0,L_{t}]\rightarrow\mathcal{S}, parameterized by arc length with total length LtL_{t}.

Finally, we execute ρt\rho_{t} in the simulator and compare measured positions and headings with the planned waypoints. We reject trajectories with collisions, blocked motion, missing waypoint records, or position or heading tracking errors reaching their respective rejection thresholds. Acceptance additionally requires completion of the entire route and a matching terminal pose. The accepted trajectory and its originating request form the paired supervision used to train the action expert.

Selecting Requests for Verified Supervision.

At each decision context, the brain samples up to NcandN_{\mathrm{cand}} candidate calls. The planner attempts grounding, trajectory planning, and execution verification, retaining the first successfully executed request. Each accepted call is grounded and planned once. Its context and verified reference trajectory form a slow-anchor training sample. Execution updates the observations before the brain generates the next call.

B.3 Constructing Action Targets from Reference Trajectories

Each slow anchor pairs the originating navigation context and movement request with an execution-verified reference trajectory. As illustrated in Figure 2 (I-b), resampling produces KK execution cycles, each with a condition Ct,kC_{t,k} and a normalized action target Ut,k⋆U_{t,k}^{\star}.

Resampling Trajectories into Execution Cycles.

For a verified reference trajectory ρt:[0,Lt]→𝒮\rho_{t}:[0,L_{t}]\rightarrow\mathcal{S} of arc length LtL_{t}, we sample N+1N+1 reference poses, yielding NN action increments. Each pose contains a planar position and heading in the world frame. We fix NN to a multiple of the execution-prefix length hh, producing K=N/hK=N/h execution cycles:

Δt=Lt/N,st,j⋆=ρt​(j​Δt),st,k⋆,fast=st,(k−1)​h⋆,K=N/h.\Delta_{t}=L_{t}/N,\hskip 9.24994pts_{t,j}^{\star}=\rho_{t}(j\Delta_{t}),\hskip 9.24994pts_{t,k}^{\star,\mathrm{fast}}=s_{t,(k-1)h}^{\star},\hskip 9.24994ptK=N/h. (16)

Here j=0,…,Nj=0,\ldots,N and k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K. The reference pose st,k⋆,fasts_{t,k}^{\star,\mathrm{fast}} identifies the remaining trajectory for cycle kk. It does not replace the agent’s actual pose when constructing the targets. Scaling Δt\Delta_{t} with trajectory length provides finer increments for short requests and larger increments for long requests.

Action Targets in the Agent’s Local Frame.

For each cycle, we translate the remaining reference positions by the agent’s actual starting position and rotate them by the negative of its actual heading. We unwrap reference headings and express them relative to this same starting heading. The first action increment runs from the actual starting pose to the first remaining reference pose. Subsequent increments are differences between successive reference poses, all expressed in the fixed coordinate frame of the cycle start. Each action comprises planar displacement and heading-increment components, with action dimension dad_{a}. We retain the next HH increments and repeat the trajectory endpoint when fewer remain, giving zero motion after the final target pose. This construction accounts for deviations between the executed pose and the reference pose rather than assuming exact reference-trajectory replay.

Normalization and Flow-Matching Supervision.

We apply fixed component-wise affine normalization to planar displacements and heading increments to obtain Ut,k⋆∈ℝH×daU_{t,k}^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}, and invert this transform to recover physical actions before execution. Normalized targets are not clipped. Flow time uu is sampled from a logit-normal distribution, and Gaussian noise ϵ\epsilon has the same shape as the complete target. The operator [⋅]j[\cdot]_{j} selects action step jj, and the expectation in Eq. (3) covers training examples, flow times, and noise. Equation (3) averages the prediction error over the h​dahd_{a} executed action components and the KK cycles of each slow anchor. All HH action tokens remain in the network input, while only the first hh positions contribute directly to the loss. Subsequent cycles supervise later motion with refreshed observations. The VLM parameters θ\theta and encoder parameters ψ\psi remain frozen during this stage. Gradients update the input queries QQ and action expert parameters ϕ\phi.

B.4 Joint Slow–Fast Policy Optimization

We detail the trajectory credit and gradient paths used by Algorithm 4.3 in Section 4.

Sharing Trajectory Returns across Decisions and Actions.

Each interaction round comprises a tool call, its execution, and the resulting feedback. We sample GG independent rollouts from the same initial navigation episode and compute undiscounted returns over all their rounds. Equation (4) subtracts the other rollouts’ mean return without standard-deviation normalization. All response tokens and executed action chunks in rollout ii receive its shared navigation credit. The reward coefficients wprogw_{\mathrm{prog}}, winfow_{\mathrm{info}}, warrw_{\mathrm{arr}}, and wsuccw_{\mathrm{succ}} are nonnegative weights for the four terms in Section 4.2. Information discovery rewards at most NinfoN_{\mathrm{info}} new entities, with total reward bounded by winfo​Ninfow_{\mathrm{info}}N_{\mathrm{info}}. The lower bound dmind_{\min} prevents the initial-distance scale from vanishing. First-arrival flags persist after the agent leaves the goal region, so only the initial entry is rewarded. Rejected or otherwise invalid calls and STOP calls receive no first-arrival reward. Turning in place cannot trigger a first positional arrival.

B.5 Tool Policy Optimization

For BB sampled rollouts, let yi,t,ny_{i,t,n} denote sampled response token nn at round tt and 𝒯i,t\mathcal{T}_{i,t} the corresponding token positions. The on-policy REINFORCE objective averages over sampled response tokens, rounds within each rollout, and the BB rollouts:

ℓ¯i,ttext\displaystyle\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{text}}_{i,t} =1|𝒯i,t|​∑n∈𝒯i,tlog⁡πθ​(yi,t,n∣xi,t,yi,t,<n),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i,t}|}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{T}_{i,t}}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t,n}\mid x_{i,t},y_{i,t,<n}), (17)
ℒtext\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{text}} =−λtextB∑i1Ti∑tsg(Ai)ℓ¯texti,t.\displaystyle=-\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{text}}}{B}\sum_{i}\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t}\operatorname{sg}(A_{i})\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{text}}_{i,t}.

Here λtext\lambda_{\mathrm{text}} weights the text objective, and sg\operatorname{sg} stops gradients through the advantage. This normalization controls the influence of response and episode length. The text branch uses an on-policy gradient without a PPO ratio.

B.6 Action Policy Optimization

The action expert policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} generates an action chunk by starting from Gaussian noise and following a stochastic Flow-SDE path conditioned on Ci,t,kC_{i,t,k}. Let ℓi,t,kexec\ell^{\mathrm{exec}}_{i,t,k} denote the log-likelihood of the sampled generation path for execution cycle kk. It sums the Gaussian transition log-probabilities over the denoising steps and all H×daH\times d_{a} action components. We clip the shared trajectory advantage from Eq. (4) to Aiexec=clip⁡(Ai,−amax,amax)A_{i}^{\mathrm{exec}}=\operatorname{clip}(A_{i},-a_{\max},a_{\max}) and assign it to every generation path in rollout ii. For a single on-policy training step, the action-policy gradient is:

∇Q,ϕℒaction=−𝔼i,t,k​[sg⁡(Aiexec)​∇Q,ϕℓi,t,kexec].\nabla_{Q,\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}=-\mathbb{E}_{i,t,k}\!\left[\operatorname{sg}(A_{i}^{\mathrm{exec}})\nabla_{Q,\phi}\ell^{\mathrm{exec}}_{i,t,k}\right]. (18)

Positive action advantages reinforce sampled generation paths, while negative advantages suppress them. The operator sg\operatorname{sg} stops gradients through the advantage. Only movement calls contribute: we average execution cycles within each call, calls within each rollout, and then rollouts. The action gradient updates QQ and ϕ\phi, propagating through the VLM to the input queries while holding the brain parameters θ\theta fixed on this path. The generation path covers the full predicted chunk, although only its first hh physical actions are executed before visual replanning. We use Euler–Maruyama integration on a uniform flow-time grid from noise at u=1u=1 to data at u=0u=0. The drift uses the signed negative time step, while the Gaussian variance uses its absolute value. Flow-SDE sampling settings are provided in Appendix D.1.

B.7 Round-Level Advantage Estimation

Section 4.1 assigns every call in rollout ii the same trajectory advantage AiA_{i}. We hold the group size GG, rewards, optimizer, and gradient paths fixed. The round-level variant replaces AiA_{i} with Ai,tA_{i,t} in both policy updates. At round tt, it compares the return remaining in rollout ii with the mean remaining return of the other rollouts for the same episode. With discount factor γ\gamma, the remaining return and round-level advantage are:

Ri,t=∑τ=tTi−1γτ−t​ri,τ,Ai,t=Ri,t−∑j≠iRj,tG−1.R_{i,t}=\sum_{\tau=t}^{T_{i}-1}\gamma^{\tau-t}r_{i,\tau},\hskip 9.24994ptA_{i,t}=R_{i,t}-\frac{\sum_{j\neq i}R_{j,t}}{G-1}. (19)

A rollout that ends before round tt contributes zero to the baseline. The comparison is aligned by interaction round, rather than by visited state or navigation progress. Rewards collected before that round are excluded from its remaining return. We use the rewards in Section 4.2 and the joint update in Section 4. The tool policy uses Ai,tA_{i,t} directly, and the action expert uses clip⁡(Ai,t,−amax,amax)\operatorname{clip}(A_{i,t},-a_{\max},a_{\max}). Algorithm B.7 summarizes this variant using the same rollout collection and separate gradient paths as Algorithm 4.3.

Appendix C Theoretical Analysis of Brain Adaptation and General Capability Retention

Section 5.2.1 shows that ZeroVLN learns navigation with substantially smaller VLM weight displacement than navigation SFT while largely retaining general visual capabilities. We analyze the mechanism behind this observation: action expert adaptation makes the base brain’s requests executable, while RL improves their use without requiring the brain to fit demonstration-defined outputs. We first compare the resulting training signals, then examine their parameter requirements and the implications for general response stability.

C.1 How SFT and RL Update the Brain

Figure 6 contrasts fitting supervised outputs with reinforcing sampled requests. To formalize this distinction, we compare their response-level gradients under the same execution conditions. For a fixed navigation context and finite response set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, let py=exp⁡(zy)/∑vexp⁡(zv)p_{y}=\exp(z_{y})/\sum_{v}\exp(z_{v}) and qyq_{y} denote the current and demonstration response probabilities. Fix the executor and continuation policy, giving each response yy an expected return RyR_{y}. Define ℒSFT=−∑yqylogpy\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\sum_{y}q_{y}\log p_{y} and J=∑ypy​RyJ=\sum_{y}p_{y}R_{y}.

Proposition 1 (Gradients of SFT and RLOO).

The SFT descent direction and expected, unnormalized RLOO ascent direction at response logit zyz_{y} are

−∂zyℒSFT=qy−py,∂zyJ=py(Ry−J).-\partial_{z_{y}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=q_{y}-p_{y},\qquad\partial_{z_{y}}J=p_{y}(R_{y}-J). (20)

Proof. Using ∂zylogpv=𝟏[v=y]−py\partial_{z_{y}}\log p_{v}=\mathbf{1}[v=y]-p_{y} gives

−∂zyℒSFT\displaystyle-\partial_{z_{y}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}} =∑vqv(𝟏[v=y]−py)=qy−py,\displaystyle=\sum_{v}q_{v}(\mathbf{1}[v=y]-p_{y})=q_{y}-p_{y}, (21)
∂zyJ\displaystyle\partial_{z_{y}}J =∑vpvRv(𝟏[v=y]−py)=py(Ry−J).\displaystyle=\sum_{v}p_{v}R_{v}(\mathbf{1}[v=y]-p_{y})=p_{y}(R_{y}-J).

For independent on-policy samples (yi,Ri)(y_{i},R_{i}) satisfying 𝔼⁡[Ri∣yi=y]=Ry\mathbb{E}[R_{i}\mid y_{i}=y]=R_{y}, the leave-one-out baseline bib_{i} is independent of the current sample. Since ∑v∇zpv=0\sum_{v}\nabla_{z}p_{v}=0, its contribution cancels in expectation Ahmadian et al. (2024):

𝔼⁡[(Ri−bi)​∇z​log⁡pyi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(R_{i}-b_{i})\nabla_{z}\log p_{y_{i}}] =∑vRv​∇zpv−𝔼⁡[bi]​∑v∇zpv=∇zJ.\displaystyle=\sum_{v}R_{v}\nabla_{z}p_{v}-\mathbb{E}[b_{i}]\sum_{v}\nabla_{z}p_{v}=\nabla_{z}J. (22)

□\square

RL selects responses by navigation value, whereas SFT also enforces a prescribed response distribution. If all responses have equal expected return, the expected RL gradient vanishes, while SFT still changes the logits whenever q≠pq\neq p. This distinction explains the training mechanisms in Figure 6. The semantic interface in Section 2 allows useful language requests to be reinforced directly, without first converting the brain’s outputs into geometric targets.

Return-Weighted Updates with Token and Round Averaging.

The tool-policy objective in Section 4 also averages over tokens and rounds. For a rollout τ\tau with TT rounds, let h⁡(τ)=T−1​∑t∇θℓ¯ttexth(\tau)=T^{-1}\sum_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\bar{\ell}_{t}^{\mathrm{text}} be its averaged token-score vector, as defined in Appendix B.5. Conditional on the same initial episode and current policies, independent grouped rollouts with finite second moments give the expected negative weighted loss gradient

gtext=λtext​𝔼​[(Ri−bi)​h​(τi)]=λtext​𝔼​[(R−𝔼​R)​(h−𝔼​h)].g_{\mathrm{text}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{text}}\mathbb{E}[(R_{i}-b_{i})h(\tau_{i})]=\lambda_{\mathrm{text}}\mathbb{E}[(R-\mathbb{E}R)(h-\mathbb{E}h)]. (23)

The identity follows from 𝔼⁡[bi​h​(τi)]=𝔼⁡[R]​𝔼​[h]\mathbb{E}[b_{i}h(\tau_{i})]=\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[h]. Along any parameter-space direction vv, the update is proportional to Cov⁡(R,v⊤​h)\operatorname{Cov}(R,v^{\top}h). Thus the implemented objective retains the same principle: the brain changes according to how its sampled tool-call paths correlate with complete navigation returns.

C.2 Why Navigation Can Require Smaller Brain Updates

The gradient comparison identifies what drives adaptation. We next examine why fitting prescribed outputs can require additional parameter change, as suggested by the SFT comparisons in Section 5.2.1. Improving navigation constrains response returns, whereas fitting demonstrations also constrains the response distribution. To compare these requirements at the same target return gain, consider a common fixed executor and the local approximation pθ0+Δ=p0+B​Δp_{\theta_{0}+\Delta}=p_{0}+B\Delta, with B=∇θpθ0B=\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta_{0}} and base parameters θ0\theta_{0}. For response-return vector RR, the local return gradient is g=B⊤​R≠0g=B^{\top}R\neq 0. A target return gain δ>0\delta>0 requires g⊤​Δ=δg^{\top}\Delta=\delta. Assume that a demonstration distribution qq is locally realizable and provides the same gain, so B​Δ=q−p0B\Delta=q-p_{0} is feasible and R⊤​(q−p0)=δR^{\top}(q-p_{0})=\delta.

Proposition 2 (Parameter Cost of Fitting Demonstrations).

In this local model, the minimum-norm change achieving the return gain is Δreturn=δ​g/‖g‖22\Delta_{\mathrm{return}}=\delta g/\|g\|_{2}^{2}. Any change ΔSFT\Delta_{\mathrm{SFT}} that fits qq satisfies

ΔSFT\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{SFT}} =Δreturn+w,g⊤w=0,\displaystyle=\Delta_{\mathrm{return}}+w,\hskip 18.49988ptg^{\top}w=0, (24)
‖ΔSFT‖22\displaystyle\|\Delta_{\mathrm{SFT}}\|_{2}^{2} =δ2‖g‖22+‖w‖22≥‖Δreturn‖22.\displaystyle=\frac{\delta^{2}}{\|g\|_{2}^{2}}+\|w\|_{2}^{2}\geq\|\Delta_{\mathrm{return}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Proof. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖Δ‖2≥δ/‖g‖2\|\Delta\|_{2}\geq\delta/\|g\|_{2} for every return-feasible change, with equality at Δreturn\Delta_{\mathrm{return}}. Demonstration fitting implies g⊤​ΔSFT=R⊤​B​ΔSFT=δg^{\top}\Delta_{\mathrm{SFT}}=R^{\top}B\Delta_{\mathrm{SFT}}=\delta. Subtracting the return-only solution gives g⊤​w=0g^{\top}w=0, and the squared-norm identity follows by orthogonality. □\square

Demonstration fitting can add parameter change that does not improve navigation return. The component ww matches the prescribed response distribution without increasing first-order return, and is nonzero whenever q−p0≠B​Δreturnq-p_{0}\neq B\Delta_{\mathrm{return}}. This gives a parameter-space explanation for the distinction in Section 5.2.1: NaVILA and DualVLN supervise particular motion commands or geometric targets, whereas ZeroVLN can reward different semantic requests that lead to effective execution. The comparison complements the distributional perspective of RL’s Razor Shenfeld et al. (2025). It characterizes local objective requirements, without assuming that RLOO attains the minimum-norm solution.

Action Expert Adaptation Reduces the Remaining Return Gap.

The frozen-brain improvements in Figure 9 show that navigation can improve by adapting execution alone. The request-grounded supervision in Section 3 uses this route before updating the brain. Let J0J_{0} be the base brain’s return with the adapted action expert and J⋆>J0J_{\star}>J_{0} the target return. The remaining gap is δ=J⋆−J0\delta=J_{\star}-J_{0}. For an actual brain-update direction dd with g⊤​d>0g^{\top}d>0, define κ=g⊤​d/(‖g‖2​‖d‖2)\kappa=g^{\top}d/(\|g\|_{2}\|d\|_{2}). The local step along dd that closes this gap has size

‖Δd‖2=J⋆−J0‖g‖2​κ.\|\Delta_{d}\|_{2}=\frac{J_{\star}-J_{0}}{\|g\|_{2}\kappa}. (25)

At fixed local return sensitivity ‖g‖2\|g\|_{2} and positive update alignment κ\kappa, raising J0J_{0} reduces the brain change required to reach J⋆J_{\star}. This connects the initialization gains in Figure 9 to the small-displacement mechanism: the action expert improves execution before RL adjusts the brain’s requests, reducing the improvement left to brain adaptation. During joint RL, the separate gradient paths in Eq. (12) preserve this division of learning by updating the brain only through the return-weighted text objective. Together, an improved initialization and the absence of prescribed-output fitting explain how our training design can support navigation learning with small brain updates.

C.3 Small Brain Updates and General-Response Stability

Section 5.2.1 evaluates both weight displacement and general visual performance. To connect these observations, we bound how a parameter change affects the expected score of sampled general-purpose responses. The frozen-brain stage leaves this response distribution unchanged on identical inputs evaluated without navigation-specific modules. The following analysis concerns the subsequent brain update during joint RL.

For a fixed general-prompt distribution μ\mu, define K(θ)=𝔼x∼μDKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πθ0(⋅∣x))K(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot\mid x)) and V⁡(θ)=𝔼x∼μ,y∼πθ​[a⁡(x,y)]V(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}[a(x,y)], where a∈[0,1]a\in[0,1] measures correctness or format validity. Let θ1=θ0+Δ\theta_{1}=\theta_{0}+\Delta. Assume common response support, twice continuous differentiability with differentiation under expectation, and ‖∇2K​(θ0+t​Δ)‖op≤M\|\nabla^{2}K(\theta_{0}+t\Delta)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq M for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1].

Bounding Changes in General-Task Performance.

Under these assumptions,

K⁡(θ1)≤M2​‖Δ‖22,|V⁡(θ1)−V⁡(θ0)|≤K⁡(θ1)/2≤M2​‖Δ‖2.K(\theta_{1})\leq\frac{M}{2}\|\Delta\|_{2}^{2},\qquad|V(\theta_{1})-V(\theta_{0})|\leq\sqrt{K(\theta_{1})/2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{M}}{2}\|\Delta\|_{2}. (26)

Proof. Since K⁡(θ0)=0K(\theta_{0})=0 and ∇K​(θ0)=0\nabla K(\theta_{0})=0, Taylor’s integral remainder gives

K⁡(θ1)=∫01(1−t)​Δ⊤​∇2K​(θ0+t​Δ)​Δ​𝑑t≤M2​‖Δ‖22.K(\theta_{1})=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\Delta^{\top}\nabla^{2}K(\theta_{0}+t\Delta)\Delta\,dt\leq\frac{M}{2}\|\Delta\|_{2}^{2}. (27)

For a∈[0,1]a\in[0,1], the score difference is bounded by total variation. Applying Pinsker’s inequality Canonne (2023) per prompt and Jensen’s inequality over μ\mu yields |V⁡(θ1)−V⁡(θ0)|≤K⁡(θ1)/2|V(\theta_{1})-V(\theta_{0})|\leq\sqrt{K(\theta_{1})/2}. □\square

Smaller brain updates tighten the bound on general-response change when sensitivity is controlled. Here V⁡(θ)V(\theta) is the expected score under stochastic decoding, so the result applies to sampled responses. The bound depends on both displacement and curvature, whose value at initialization is the Fisher information Martens (2020). Relative displacement ϵ=‖Δ‖2/‖θ0‖2\epsilon=\|\Delta\|_{2}/\|\theta_{0}\|_{2} enters through ‖Δ‖2=ϵ​‖θ0‖2\|\Delta\|_{2}=\epsilon\|\theta_{0}\|_{2}. This connects the parameter comparison in Figure 7 to the capability analysis in Section 5.2.1, while Table 7 measures the retained behavior directly.

Our central insight is to reduce what the brain must relearn to navigate. The semantic interface preserves its native request space, action expert adaptation makes those requests executable, and joint RL improves their navigation value without matching prescribed geometric outputs. The analysis explains how this division can reduce the required brain change and, under bounded sensitivity, support stable general responses. It provides a theoretical account of the main-text finding that ZeroVLN acquires navigation skills while largely retaining the base brain’s general capabilities.

Appendix D Experimental Setup and Baselines

D.1 Training Data and Optimization Settings

Action Expert Architecture and Parameter Counts.

Figure 3 and Tables 2 and 3 summarize the implementation of the architecture in Appendix B.1. The semantic and visual branches provide 16 and 32 tokens, respectively. The flow-time MLP adds one token to their concatenation, forming a 49-token cross-attention memory. Flow integration uses three steps. Each movement call permits up to four execution cycles. The 34.784M trainable action expert parameters comprise 0.792M in the semantic adapter, 3.365M in the visual adapter and pooler, 1.774M in condition fusion, 0.000768M in channel embeddings, and 28.852M in the velocity network. We load only the vision tower from Qwen3.5-4B. Open-loop adaptation updates the contextual queries and action expert with the brain and visual encoder frozen. Joint RL additionally updates the brain through the text objective.

Request-Grounded Training Data.

Table 4 gives the episode and anchor counts for each dataset. We count each distinct scene, episode ID, and instruction as one source episode. The brain generates two candidate calls per decision and samples two more (Ncand=4N_{\mathrm{cand}}=4 in total) if neither passes the verification procedure in Appendix B.2. We retain execution-verified movement calls with four complete execution cycles and at least 0.1 m of accumulated translation. The planner records 65 poses along each reference trajectory. Keeping every fourth pose gives 17 poses and 16 action increments, divided into four execution cycles. ZeroVLN (w/o RL) denotes the action-expert-adapted checkpoint used to initialize RL and serves as the No RL baseline in the update-scope ablation.

Trajectory Planner Settings.

For the planner in Appendix B.2, we use a preferred standoff distance d0=0.3​md_{0}=0.3\,\mathrm{m}, visibility weight λv=1\lambda_{v}=1, and distance weight λd=2\lambda_{d}=2, with distances measured in meters. Selected endpoints must lie within 0.9​m0.9\,\mathrm{m} of the object’s bounding box. A* searches an eight-connected occupancy grid with preferred clearance c0=0.6​mc_{0}=0.6\,\mathrm{m} and clearance weight λc=0.8\lambda_{c}=0.8. We fall back to the ordinary shortest grid path if the clearance-aware route is more than 25%25\% longer. Smoothing is weakened if it increases path length by more than 5%5\% or reduces minimum clearance by more than 0.05​m0.05\,\mathrm{m}. Execution verification rejects position errors reaching 0.035​m0.035\,\mathrm{m} or heading errors reaching 2∘2^{\circ}.

Open-Loop Adaptation and Joint RL Settings.

Both training stages use AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, numerical epsilon 10−810^{-8}, and no learning-rate warmup. Weight decay is 0.01 during open-loop adaptation and zero during RL. Open-loop training runs on four 16-device nodes, with one slow anchor per device per training step, a global batch of 64 anchors, and gradient clipping at 1. Each anchor contains four execution cycles. We sample SAGE-3D, R2R, and RxR at a ratio of 1:1:2 in open-loop training and optimize the queries and action expert at a constant learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}. For flow-matching supervision, the logit-normal flow-time distribution uses an underlying normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Each epoch contains 6,014 training steps. The RL initialization follows 10,826 training steps, or approximately 1.8 epochs. RL uses eight 16-device nodes and samples the datasets at a ratio of 2:1:1. Each training step contains 64 episodes with eight rollouts each, totaling 512 rollouts. The brain, queries, and action expert use a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, while the fast visual backbone remains frozen. The RL training budget is 200 training steps. We set the return discount γ=1\gamma=1 for both credit estimators, the text-loss weight λtext=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{text}}=0.1, and the action-advantage clipping threshold amax=1a_{\max}=1. Distance progress, first arrival, and terminal success each have weight 1. We set Ninfo=5N_{\mathrm{info}}=5 and winfo=0.01w_{\mathrm{info}}=0.01, capping the information reward at 0.05 per episode. Distance progress uses dmin=1​md_{\min}=1\,\mathrm{m}. The action sampler uses three uniform Flow-SDE transitions from u=1u=1 through u=2/3u=2/3 and u=1/3u=1/3 to u=0u=0, with noise scale 0.08. The drift step is −1/3-1/3, and the Gaussian variance uses its absolute value. The numerical variance floor is 10−610^{-6}. The main single-training-step action objective is evaluated at the rollout policy, as in Eq. (18).

Context Management.

The brain has a 131,072-token context limit, with thinking disabled throughout collection, RL, and navigation evaluation. Supervision collection uses temperature 1.0 and top-pp 0.95, with a 256-token text budget. RL sampling uses temperature 1.0, top-pp 1.0, no top-kk truncation or repetition, presence, or frequency penalties, and a 512-token completion limit per round. Navigation evaluation uses temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95, with a 256-token text budget excluding reserved query tokens. Action expert data collection and RL allow 100 and 50 rounds per episode, respectively. On SAGE-3D, the navigation camera provides 640×\times480 RGB observations with a horizontal field of view of 115∘115^{\circ} at a height of 1.2 m. We append tool calls, execution feedback, and observations to the interaction history. Only the final image of a movement call is appended as the next slow observation, separately from the tool result that reports motion and execution status. Intermediate images condition fast execution. During long evaluation episodes, history is compressed only when the input, output budget, and an 8,192-token reserve exceed the service window. Compression retains the initial task and recent eight rounds, samples one complete round from every four older rounds, and removes older past-trajectory snapshots while preserving the latest cumulative trajectory. Retained calls remain paired with their feedback and observations. Original round indices identify gaps in the sampled history.

Comparing Execution-Prefix and Full-Sequence Supervision.

Figure 9 compares Execution-Prefix Supervision and Full-Sequence Supervision on identical reference trajectories with the brain frozen. Both variants use 100 fixed episodes per dataset and four rollouts per episode, each with a 100-round budget. SR averages the outcomes of these rollouts. Pass@4 counts an episode as successful when at least one of its four rollouts succeeds. With the data, initialization, training settings, and evaluation held fixed, only the supervised action positions change: both variants predict 16 actions and execute four, while the flow-matching loss covers either the first four or all 16 actions (Section 3). Figure 5 uses 1,000 sampled training anchors per dataset. The high frequency of short reference trajectories reflects the collection threshold: over half of the trajectories in the 0.1–0.3 m bin lie within 1 cm of 0.1 m. Lengths up to 2 mm below this cutoff are included in the first bin.

Evaluating Credit Assignment, Joint Updates, and Rewards.

The upper row of Figure 12 compares update scopes using trajectory-level credit. The lower row compares reward ablations under the same trajectory-level credit assignment. Figure 13 additionally reports update-scope and reward ablations using round-level advantage estimation. All variants start from the same action-expert-adapted checkpoint. Each evaluation uses one rollout on each of 100 fixed episodes per dataset and a 100-round budget. In Figure 12, SR and NE are averaged equally over R2R and RxR, while SPL is averaged equally over SAGE-3D, R2R, and RxR. Its OSR is the equal-weight mean of SAGE-3D arrival success and R2R/RxR OSR. The direct credit-assignment comparison in Section 5.3 holds rewards and update settings fixed and compares round-level and trajectory-level advantage estimation. In Figure 11, all four metrics (SR, OSR, SPL, and NE) are averaged equally over R2R and RxR, and the OSR–SR gap is computed from these same averages. Together, these three ablations test how credit coordinates decisions across rounds, whether both policies need to adapt, and which reward signals sustain navigation learning.

D.2 Why Supervision Should Follow the Brain’s Requests

We examine why the action expert should learn from the brain’s actual requests, as proposed in Section 3. The alternatives expose two distinct mismatches: constructed requests can differ from the brain’s language, and fixed demonstration trajectories can differ from its intended movement.

Constructed Requests Do Not Guarantee Navigation Transfer.

We design request augmentation to make the action expert distinguish movement intentions under identical visual observations, rather than predict motion from the scene alone. Inspired by CAST Glossop et al. (2025), we construct paired movement requests at the same navigation state while keeping the brain frozen (Table 5). Direction augmentation pairs leftward and rightward diagonal trajectories with corresponding language templates in the tool call’s plan field. Object/relation augmentation changes the requested object or the side from which it is approached, pairing each request with its corresponding geometrically verified trajectory. We retain the original data and add these request–trajectory pairs to train the contextual queries and action expert. On 67 held-out state pairs evaluated with four shared noise seeds, the action expert learns these requests well: paired direction accuracy rises from 0% to 95.90% on the training template and reaches 96.27% on a held-out template (Table 6). Yet high template accuracy does not translate into better closed-loop navigation. On the same 100 SAGE-3D episodes with four rollouts per episode and a 50-call budget, final navigation SR is 13.25%, equal to training without augmentation, despite direction accuracy remaining above 92% in Figure 15a,b. These augmentation runs use one training seed and different training exposure.

Request Distribution Matters beyond Geometric Validity.

Among 456 brain-generated requests evaluated with the same four noise seeds, 199 groups contain both left and right movement requests under the same state and request family. Paired heading accuracy on these 199 pairs is 64.70% without augmentation and 56.91% with augmentation (Table 6). These requests also differ from the templates: none of the 456 sampled plans uses the explicit diagonal-motion terms employed in direction augmentation. Thus, an action expert can learn the constructed language–motion associations without reliably transferring them to the language used during navigation. The missing alignment concerns how the brain expresses its intention, not merely whether the supervised trajectory is feasible. This motivates collecting requests from the frozen brain itself, so action expert adaptation targets the language it will encounter during interaction.

For the paired tests in Table 6, constructed requests require correct lateral directions, at least 5 cm displacement, and collision-free static replay; brain-generated requests require correct heading directions in both prediction prefixes. In Figure 15a,b, direction and object/relation tests use 67 and 25 pairs, respectively, with four samples per pair. Object/relation tests require collision-free motion, trajectory error below 0.5 m, and closer agreement with the requested branch. The dashed line denotes training without augmentation. Curves connect evaluated policies without smoothing.

Natural Requests Need Corresponding Motion Targets.

GT-Route Anchoring aims to combine the brain’s natural request distribution with readily available expert trajectories, avoiding the need to plan a new trajectory for every request. We first place slow anchors along dataset-provided expert trajectories. At each anchor, the frozen brain receives the navigation instruction, current and historical RGB observations, previous tool interactions, and the past trajectory trace, then generates a movement call with target, where, and plan arguments. The brain does not see the future expert trajectory. We sample eight calls per anchor and retain up to four valid, deduplicated history branches without filtering calls by their directional agreement with the trajectory. Each retained call is paired with the original trajectory’s subsequent action labels, and the next anchor’s observations and execution feedback are obtained by replaying that trajectory. Thus, the expert trajectory determines the visited states and motion targets, while the brain generates the requests from those states. Different requests can consequently receive the same motion target. Request-Grounded Anchoring instead plans a reference trajectory for each generated request. Figure 15c,d compares the complete pipelines on 100 episodes each: GT-Route Anchoring uses one rollout per episode with 200 calls, while Request-Grounded Anchoring uses four rollouts with 100 calls. The best-SR GT-Route policy reaches 34.0% SR and 21.55% SPL, while our RL initialization reaches 37.5% and 22.56%, with differences in episode subsets, contexts, executors, and training exposure between the pipelines.

Together, these comparisons motivate an open-loop training scheme that aligns both the source of requests and their motion targets. Constructed requests can teach local control without transferring to the brain’s language, while attaching natural requests to fixed expert trajectories does not ensure that the labels execute those requests. Our key design choice is to let the frozen brain’s requests determine the supervision: the planner constructs a corresponding reference trajectory, allowing the action expert to learn the movements the brain actually asks it to perform. Execution-prefix supervision further aligns this learning with visual replanning, supported by the matched-trajectory comparison in Figure 9. This request-to-trajectory construction enables semantic action expert adaptation without navigation SFT of the brain or dataset-provided expert trajectories.

D.3 Direct Tool Use Baseline

We evaluate the original Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint using four simulator-executed tools: move_forward(distance), move_backward(distance), turn(direction, degrees), and stop(reason). The VLM receives no navigation SFT or RL. Forward and backward requests specify a distance between 0.05 and 5 m, and turning requests specify left or right rotation between 0.5∘0.5^{\circ} and 90∘90^{\circ}. The harness executes translations in substeps of at most 0.25 m and returns the actual movement, blocked status, and updated RGB observation. Each response permits one tool call. Invalid or multiple calls receive error feedback and consume one decision before the model retries.

The model observes the task instruction, up to eight recent RGB images including the current view, textual tool history, and the latest diagram of its executed trajectory. The diagram is built from actual relative movement and heading, with markers for blocked motion and collisions. Goal coordinates, reference routes, and evaluator success signals are withheld from the policy. Sampling uses temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95, with thinking disabled and a maximum of 256 output tokens per decision. We run one rollout per episode on all 944 SAGE-3D, 1,839 R2R, and 3,669 English RxR episodes. Each episode allows up to 200 interaction rounds. Appendix G.2 presents the baseline instructions in English along with its tool schemas.

D.4 Controlled Comparisons with SFT-Based VLN Baselines

We use the official open-source implementations of NaVILA Cheng et al. (2024) and DualVLN Wei et al. (2025a), replacing only their VLM backbones and training episodes with the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone and 34,445 source episodes used by ZeroVLN, while preserving their original data augmentation, supervision construction, training procedures, action representations, and motion scales. NaVILA expands the source demonstrations into 1,305,082 motion-command samples and fine-tunes the full VLM backbone for one epoch with a global batch size of 64. DualVLN retains its two-stage procedure of first learning pixel-goal prediction, then freezing the brain and training a continuous-action expert. The two stages use 1,539,344 and 1,126,788 distinct supervision samples and complete 12,027 and 8,804 training steps, respectively, with a global batch size of 128. Continuation uses previously unused samples and covers the full eligible fast-policy sample pool. NaVILA’s supervision sample count is 3.39 times our semantic anchor count, while DualVLN’s two stages use 4.00 and 2.93 times as many samples, respectively. Our comparison thus uses the same backbone and source data while preserving both baselines’ native pipelines for expanding supervision, without restricting their sample counts to the number of semantic anchors used by ZeroVLN.

D.5 Measuring General Capabilities and Weight Displacement

We evaluate the shared Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, ZeroVLN, DualVLN, and NaVILA on twelve general visual and spatial benchmarks. Table 7 provides the complete results. Weight displacement measures the extent of parameter change, while benchmark performance evaluates the preservation of general response capabilities, providing complementary evidence at the parameter and functional levels.

Shared Inputs and Scoring Criteria.

All four models receive the same evaluation examples, images, questions, answer options, and benchmark-specific prompts through VLMEvalKit, without navigation system prompts or tool schemas. We use temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.8, top-kk 20, a maximum output length of 32,768 tokens, and seed 3407, with thinking disabled. The presence and repetition penalties are 1.5 and 1.0, respectively, and min-pp is 0. Each benchmark uses the same answer parser and scoring rules across models. Multiple-choice answers are extracted and scored with the rule-based exact_matching evaluator rather than an LLM judge. Spatial localization answers follow the corresponding benchmark’s native scoring rules. For example, the EmbSpatialBench prompt requests the selected option letter in a JSON answer field. We report the vanilla score for 3DSRBench and average the twelve benchmark scores with equal weights.

Relative Weight Displacement.

We represent navigation adaptation as a task vector, following Ilharco et al. Ilharco et al. (2022). Let θpre\theta_{\mathrm{pre}} contain the inherited VLM weights before navigation adaptation and θft\theta_{\mathrm{ft}} the corresponding weights after adaptation, including RL for ZeroVLN. Li et al. Xuhong et al. (2018) use the base weights as the reference for an L2L_{2} penalty in transfer learning. Building on these definitions, we normalize the weight difference by the base model’s norm and report the relative displacement as a percentage:

Δ​θ=θft−θpre,drel=100​‖Δ​θ‖2‖θpre‖2%.\Delta\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{ft}}-\theta_{\mathrm{pre}},\hskip 18.49988ptd_{\mathrm{rel}}=100\,\frac{\|\Delta\theta\|_{2}}{\|\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}\|_{2}}\%. (28)

We match saved checkpoint tensors by parameter name and shape and accumulate squared weight differences and squared base-weight values in double precision. The square root of their ratio gives the relative L2L_{2} displacement. We include all inherited VLM weights, including frozen weights, and count shared parameters once. New contextual queries and action heads are excluded because they have no counterpart in the base VLM. All three methods use the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B initialization as the reference.

Appendix E Further Evaluation of Navigation and General Capabilities

E.1 Comprehensive General Capability Evaluation

Table 7 provides the individual results behind the general capability analysis in Section 5.2.1. With the same backbone and training episodes, ZeroVLN matches or exceeds the base score on ten of twelve benchmarks; NaVILA and DualVLN score zero under the shared free-form evaluation. Appendix D.5 specifies the prompts, decoding settings, and scoring criteria.

Answer-Choice Readout Details.

The controlled readout in Figure 8 uses the same 100 questions per benchmark for all four brains. We extract next-token probabilities immediately after the fixed Answer: prefix and compare only the tokens for that question’s valid option labels (e.g., A and B for a two-choice question). The highest-probability valid label is scored against the ground truth, regardless of how much probability the model assigns to other tokens. MMSI-Bench uses the non-circular setting. Across the 700 paired questions, the base brain, ZeroVLN, NaVILA, and DualVLN answer 440, 434, 280, and 255 correctly, respectively. The mean random baseline is 32.48%. Section 5.2.1 analyzes these results alongside the free-form evaluation.

E.2 Trajectory Consistency Evaluation Details

This experiment expands Section 5.4 by testing request-conditioned execution under matched inputs before and after joint RL. We compare the action-expert-adapted policy with the joint-RL policy on 1,000 movement requests from SAGE-3D training episodes. We rank episode identities by their SHA-256 hashes and select one accepted request per episode, using its first execution cycle. Both policies receive identical archived observations and requests, with one prediction per request generated using the same noise seed. The comparison evaluates the first four predicted action steps, matching the executed prefix in Section 3.

We measure the distance between the predicted four-step prefix endpoint and the corresponding four-step reference-prefix endpoint in the agent’s local frame. The reference-prefix endpoint serves as the local goal for the evaluated execution cycle. Angular deviation measures the angle between the predicted and reference net-displacement vectors over these same four steps. To avoid unstable direction estimates for near-zero motion, we require both vectors to have a magnitude of at least 0.05 m and retain the same valid requests for both policies. This yields 804 paired requests in Figure 14.

Appendix F Case Studies of Feedback-Guided Navigation

We expand the recovery example in Section 5.2 and present seven successful evaluation rollouts of ZeroVLN to illustrate how the brain uses visual feedback to revise movement requests, inspect landmarks, and decide when to stop. The figures pair selected observations with the subsequent tool calls and overlay executed paths on horizontal sections of the corresponding Matterport3D scene meshes in the agent’s starting coordinate frame. Multi-level maps overlay scene sections from the relevant floors. Each decision panel shows the path executed before its call. Each case reports success, SPL, navigation error, executed path length, and the number of tool calls. The green triangle and red dot mark the start and current position, respectively. All maps within a case share the same planar coordinates and scale.

R2R: Revising Requests after Blocked Motion.

In Figure 10, the agent must leave the room, climb the stairs, and stop on the second landing. At round 15, the brain asks the action expert to climb the next flight, and the call returns blocked. It turns left at round 16 and retries, receiving another blocked response at round 17. After another view change, the movement call toward the second landing at round 19 completes its allotted action steps. The brain continues to use movement and view changes before issuing STOP at round 25.

RxR: Confirming the Goal with Landmarks.

In Figure 16, the instruction describes a lamp with three portraits on the right and a bed on the left. At round 20, the brain asks the action expert to approach the lamp on the nightstand, and the call returns blocked. The brain turns left and reissues the request from the new view. It then turns right and issues STOP at round 24, citing the lamp, portraits, and bed in its stop call.

R2R: Inspecting an Exit before Moving Outdoors.

In Figure 17, the brain requests a route past the TV toward the sliding glass door. After turning right to inspect the exit, it directs the action expert toward the patio at round 16 and issues STOP outside at round 26.

R2R: Refining Requests to Locate the Goal.

In Figure 18, the brain first delegates movement through the nearest doorway. It turns to inspect the room, then requests an approach to the toilet at round 8 and refines the direction at round 10. It issues STOP once the toilet room is in view at round 12.

RxR: Recognizing the Goal from Visual Landmarks.

In Figure 19, the brain turns around to leave the washroom and later uses the foot of the bed as a local waypoint. It turns left at round 32 and cites the white shelves when issuing STOP at round 39.

RxR: Following a Sequence of Landmarks.

In Figure 20, the instruction links a hallway, staircase, dining table, glass door, and a wall with a white clock. The brain requests movement toward the staircase at round 6, downstairs at round 10, and toward the dining table and glass door at rounds 14 and 18. It issues STOP at the clock wall at round 22. The executed path is 17.87 m with SPL 0.951.

R2R: Coordinating Climbing and Goal Confirmation.

In Figure 21, the agent must climb the stairs and wait at the top. The brain delegates successive climbing requests, turns to inspect the upper landing at round 14, and issues STOP at round 17. The executed path is 11.21 m with SPL 1.000.

Appendix G Navigation System Prompts

We present the system prompts for ZeroVLN and Direct Tool Use with shared wording for observation interpretation and tool-call formatting. Their tool definitions and history handling follow the respective interfaces in Section 2 and Appendix D.3. The Direct Tool Use prompt is translated from the Chinese evaluation prompt into English for presentation.
